--- title: 'MATH 4025: Classification + Logistic Regression' --- ## Concept Check - Regression is what we call it if we're trying to predict a quantitative target variables. What do we call it when we are trying to predict a categorical target variable? - Is this a type of supervised or unsupervised learning? - When we fit a model we use our (training/test) set but when we evaluate our model we make predictions on our (training/test) set and use those predictions to compute our performance metrics. ## Classification Problems {.smaller} - Response $Y$ is qualitative (categorical). - Objective: build a classifier $\hat{Y}=\hat{C}(\mathbf{X})$ + assigns class label to a future unlabeled (unseen) observations + understand the relationship between the predictors and response - Two ways to make predictions + Class probabilities + Class labels ## Today: Binary Classification - **Binary Classification:** response variable has only two categorical (e.g. win/lose, yes/no, etc.) - Typically: choose one categorical to call **success** (1) and one category to call **failure** (0). - Success doesn't have to be a good thing (success is frequently *death*) and failure doesn't have to be bad. - Choice of success vs. failure doesn't matter, your resulting model will be the same, but you will need to know which category is which to interpret your results ## Default Dataset {.smaller} A simulated data set containing information on ten thousand customers. The aim here is to predict which customers will default on their credit card debt. We will consider `default` as the response variable. Let do the following: 1. Load the data 2. Split the data 3. Summarize the response variable 4. Use `.info()` to look at the data types. ## Data Types in Python {.smaller} - `object` / `string`: often used for categorical data in pandas. - `category`: Efficient storage for categorical data (similar to R's factor). - `pandas` categorical type allows defining order of categories, useful for plotting. - When modeling in `scikit-learn`, we often need to convert qualitative variables to dummy variables (One-Hot Encoding) unless the specific library handles them. ## K-Nearest Neighbors Classifier - Given a value for $K$ and a test data point $x_0$: $$P(Y=j | X=x_0)=\dfrac{1}{K} \sum_{x_i \in \mathcal{N}_0} I(y_i = j)$$ where $\mathcal{N}_0$ is the set of the $K$ "closest" neighbors. - For classification: neighbors "vote" for class (unlike in regression where predictions are obtained by averaging) $$P(Y=j | X=x_0)=\text{Proportion of neighbors in class }j$$ ## Practice Let's build a K-Nearest Neighbors Classifier to predict `default` from `balance`. ## K-Nearest Neighbors Classifier: Predictions - `predict` with a categorical response: - Two different ways of making predictions in `scikit-learn`: - `predict()`: returns class labels - `predict_proba()`: returns probabilities ## Practice! Let's practice predicting class labels and probabilities. Bonus: Let's investigate the `weights` argument in `KNeighborsClassifier`. # Logistic Regression ## Why Not Linear Regression? {.smaller} ::: {#303d688f .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Create 0/1 variable for Linear Regression Default_lr = Default_train.copy() Default_lr['default_0_1'] = np.where(Default_lr['default'] == 'Yes', 1, 0) lrfit = LinearRegression() lrfit.fit(Default_lr[['balance']], Default_lr['default_0_1']) # Predict on training data preds = lrfit.predict(Default_lr[['balance']]) show(pd.DataFrame({'balance': Default_lr['balance'], 'pred': preds}).head()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## Why Not Linear Regression? {.smaller} ::: {#9782b430 .cell fig.align='center' execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ![](08-classification-logistic_files/figure-revealjs/cell-4-output-1.png){width=960 height=480} ::: ::: - Linear regression: does not model probabilities well + might produce probabilities less than zero or bigger than one + treats increase from 0.41 to 0.5 as same as 0.01 to 0.1 (bad) ## Why Not Linear Regression? Suppose we have a response, $$Y=\begin{cases} 1 & \text{if stroke} \\ 2 & \text{if drug overdose} \\ 3 & \text{if epileptic seizure} \end{cases}$$ - Linear regression suggests an ordering, and in fact implies that the differences between classes have meaning + e.g. drug overdose $-$ stroke $= 1$? 🤔 ## Logistic Regression {.smaller} Consider a one-dimensional binary classification problem: - Transform the linear model $\beta_0 + \beta_1 \ X$ so that the output is a probability - Use **logistic** function: $$g(t)=\dfrac{e^t}{1+e^t} \ \ \ \text{for} \ t \in \mathcal{R}$$ - Then: $$p(X)=P(Y=1|X) = P(\text{Success}| X)=g\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 \ X\right)=\dfrac{e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 \ X}}{1+e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 \ X}}$$ ## Other important quantities - **Odds**: $\dfrac{p(x)}{1-p(x)}$ - **Log-Odds (logit)**: $\log\left(\dfrac{p(x)}{1-p(x)}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \ X$ + Linear function of predictors - Suppose the probability of success is 50%, what should $p(x)$, your odds, and your log-odds be? ## Logistic Regression ::: {#ce4da4fe .cell execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ![](08-classification-logistic_files/figure-revealjs/cell-5-output-1.png){width=960 height=480} ::: ::: ## Fitting the model Let's fit a logistic regression model predicting `default` using `balance` and investigate the coefficients. ## Interpreting Coefficients - As $X$ increases by 1, the log-odds increase by $\hat{\beta}_1$ + I.e. probability of default increases but NOT linearly + Change in the probability of default due to a one-unit change in balance depends on the current balance value ## Interpreting Coefficients ::: {#449bdcb5 .cell execution_count=5} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ![](08-classification-logistic_files/figure-revealjs/cell-6-output-1.png){width=960 height=480} ::: ::: ## Making predictions: Theory {.smaller} For `balance`=\$700, ::: {.incremental} - $\hat{p}(X)=\dfrac{e^{\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1 X}}{1+e^{\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1 X}}=\dfrac{e^{\text{intercept} + (\text{coef} \times 700)}}{1+e^{\text{intercept} + (\text{coef} \times 700)}}$ - Using our values: Intercept $\approx -10.20$, Coef $\approx 0.0052$ - $$p(700) \approx \dfrac{e^{-10.20 + 3.64}}{1+e^{-10.20 + 3.64}} \approx 0.0014$$ - $$\textbf{Odds}(X) = \dfrac{\hat{p}(X)}{1-\hat{p}(X)} \approx 0.0014$$ - $$\textbf{Log-Odds}(X) = \approx -6.57$$ ::: ## Practice Let's generate our predicted classes and probability for our test set in Python. # Recap ## Key Takeaways - **Classification**: Predicting a categorical response variable (qualitative). - **KNN Classifier**: Assigns class labels or probabilities based on the proportion of neighbors in each class (majority vote). - **Logistic Regression**: - Used for binary classification to ensure predicted probabilities are between 0 and 1. - Models the **log-odds (logit)** as a linear function of the predictors. - **Interpretation**: Coefficients $\beta$ represent the change in log-odds for a one-unit increase in the predictor, which corresponds to a non-linear change in probability.
